I moved the WebSocket connection, protobuf decoding, and sorting index completely off the main thread into a dedicated Web Worker writing normalized numeric columns directly into a pre-allocated `SharedArrayBuffer` backed by `Float64Array` and `Int32Array` views—eliminating per-tick object allocations and structured-clone serialization overhead. On the UI thread, I replaced standard React state subscriptions with a custom virtualizer that only mounted the ~35 visible DOM rows in the viewport and polled a dirty-bitmask in the `SharedArrayBuffer` once per `requestAnimationFrame` tick, mutating changed cell `textContent` directly via refs when scrolling was idle. A key tradeoff was requiring Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (`COOP`) and `COEP` headers to enable `SharedArrayBuffer`, which meant proxying a third-party analytics script through our CDN. answers.text: Our marketing team previously sent $15 renewal discount emails to the top 20% highest-risk subscribers scored by an XGBoost churn propensity model, yet an A/B holdout showed near-zero net retention lift and high subsidy waste. question.question: In your legal contract RAG pipeline, how did you diagnose and fix retrieval failures on cross-reference clauses, and why did you choose that chunking and reranking architecture?

Error analysis showed two root causes: dense embeddings missed exact defined terms and section numbers (like 'Indemnification Cap under Section 8.4(b)'), and fixed token splits severed child clauses from the parent section header defining their scope and exceptions. I redesigned ingestion using an AST parser over Markdown-converted PDFs to build a two-level hierarchical index: small 256-token leaf chunks prepended with their full ancestor breadcrumb header path (e.g., `[Article VIII > Section 8.4 Indemnification > (b) Basket]`) linked to full parent sections stored in Postgres. For first-stage retrieval, I combined sparse BM25 (to catch exact clause identifiers and defined legal entities) with dense `bge-m3` embeddings via Reciprocal Rank Fusion ($k=60$) to pull the top 40 leaf candidates, then passed those 40 into a cross-encoder (`rerank-english-v3.0`) to select the top 5 and hydrated their parent sections for generation. We rejected LLM-based query expansion because it added 900ms latency, whereas our RRF + cross-encoder pipeline added only 115ms p95 while boosting Recall@5 from 61% to 89% and cutting hallucinated citations by two-thirds.

question.question: How did you architect the migration from long-lived static AWS IAM keys to SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity across your multi-cluster Kubernetes and bare-metal fleet without breaking active traffic?
question.rationale: Tests zero-trust architecture depth, X.509/JWT-SVID attestation mechanics, federation with cloud IAM, and zero-downtime dual-auth rollout strategy.
question.anchor: eliminated 1,200 static IAM secrets by deploying SPIRE federated OIDC workload attestation across EKS and on-prem bare-metal nodes

answers.label: excellent
answers.text: We had 1,200 static AWS IAM user keys injected via Vault into both EKS pods and legacy on-prem bare-metal services, creating a severe credential-exfiltration blast radius and manual 90-day rotation toil. Standard EKS IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) couldn't solve this alone because 35% of workloads ran on bare-metal Linux hosts outside AWS. I architected a unified identity plane using SPIFFE/SPIRE with hierarchical nested SPIRE servers: node attestation used the AWS Instance Identity Document on EKS and TPM 2.0 hardware endorsement keys (`devid`) on bare metal, while workload attestation verified Kubernetes service-account UIDs and Linux kernel cgroup/binary SHA-256 hashes. question.question: How did you design the offline-first sync engine in your iOS field technician app to handle conflict resolution when technicians edited the same work order without cellular connectivity?
question.rationale: Evaluates practical mobile persistence architecture (SQLite/GRDB), mutation outbox patterns, deterministic conflict resolution, and battery/network efficiency.

answers.label: excellent
answers.text: Our field technicians regularly spent four to six hours underground in utility vaults with zero cellular coverage while multiple crew members updated the same work order on iPads. Previously, the app used whole-record REST `PUT` overwrites from CoreData when connectivity returned, meaning whoever gained signal second silently clobbered their partner's inspection checklist and photo attachments. I replaced the persistence layer with SQLite via GRDB in WAL mode and designed a field-level Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) state-based CRDT combined with an append-only local mutation outbox. Rather than syncing full JSON blobs, every UI edit recorded an atomic `{entity_id, field_path, value, hlc_timestamp, device_id}` delta in the outbox table and updated the local projection immediately for instant UI responsiveness. We chose HLCs over raw wall-clock timestamps because technicians frequently had drifted device clocks, and over full Operational Transformation because work order schemas were structured key-value fields rather than free-form collaborative text. On `NWPathMonitor` connectivity restoration, a `BGProcessingTask` drained deltas in idempotent batches; orthogonal fields merged automatically, while true concurrent edits to the same scalar field resolved deterministically via HLC and flagged a non-blocking audit badge. This reduced sync data-loss tickets from ~40/month to zero.

Because updates were tracked per field with HLC ordering, two technicians editing different parts of the same work order merged cleanly without any data loss.

cases.role_context: Senior Backend Engineer — Distributed Storage & Databases

question.question: Explain the difference between PostgreSQL's `READ COMMITTED` and `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation) transaction isolation levels, what anomalies still occur under `REPEATABLE READ`, and how that impacted your inventory reservation service.
question.rationale: Tests precise conceptual grasp of MVCC snapshot semantics, write skew anomalies vs lost updates, and grounding in their concrete inventory service.
question.anchor: prevented flash-sale overselling in Postgres inventory service by resolving write-skew anomaly between concurrent reservation checks

answers.label: excellent
answers.text: In PostgreSQL's MVCC engine, both `READ COMMITTED` and `REPEATABLE READ` rely on non-blocking transaction snapshots, but they differ in snapshot lifecycle and conflict detection. Under `READ COMMITTED` (the default), Postgres takes a fresh snapshot at the start of each individual SQL statement within a transaction, allowing non-repeatable reads and phantom reads if another transaction commits between statements. Under `REPEATABLE READ`—which Postgres implements as Snapshot Isolation—a single snapshot is frozen at the first non-control statement of the transaction, guaranteeing repeatable reads and preventing standard lost updates because Postgres aborts the transaction with `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update` if a target row was modified after the snapshot began. However, `REPEATABLE READ` does NOT prevent **write skew**, where two concurrent transactions read overlapping row sets satisfying an invariant and then modify disjoint rows, violating the invariant upon commit. In our flash-sale inventory service, warehouse stock was sharded across bin rows (`bin_A=1`, `bin_B=1`) with an invariant that total reserved stock across bins could not exceed `total_available - safety_buffer`. Two concurrent `REPEATABLE READ` transactions both saw total stock = 2 and decremented separate bins without row-level conflict, overselling by 1. We fixed this by locking the parent SKU summary row via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (choosing explicit pessimistic row locking over full `SERIALIZABLE` SSI to avoid high retry-storm latency at 2,000 RPS).

answers.label: adequate
answers.text: In PostgreSQL, `READ COMMITTED` takes a new data snapshot for every individual query inside a transaction, so if another transaction commits in between, a second `SELECT` can see different data. `REPEATABLE READ` takes one snapshot at the start of the first query and keeps it for the whole transaction, and it automatically aborts if two transactions try to update the exact same row concurrently. However, `REPEATABLE READ` still allows write skew, where two transactions read the same set of rows to check a business rule and then update different rows. In our inventory reservation service, this caused flash-sale overselling when concurrent workers updated separate bin records, which we solved using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks.

When designing scalable e-commerce and inventory management platforms, engineers must carefully balance data consistency guarantees against system throughput and query latency. Isolation levels essentially control how transactions interact with each other when multiple users are reading and writing data at the same time in a multi-threaded environment. Higher isolation levels provide stronger protection against concurrency bugs and race conditions by restricting how uncommitted or concurrent data changes become visible across sessions, whereas lower isolation levels prioritize performance and concurrency by relaxing locking constraints. In our inventory service, ensuring that database transactions were properly configured and indexed was critical for maintaining accurate stock counts and delivering a seamless checkout experience during high-traffic promotional events.

question.question: Explain why TCP head-of-line blocking occurs in HTTP/2 over a single connection despite stream multiplexing, how gRPC load balancing in Kubernetes is affected by it, and how you resolved it on your telemetry ingestion tier.
question.rationale: Evaluates deep networking fundamentals (L4 vs L7 multiplexing, TCP congestion window/retransmit stalling all streams) tied directly to their Kubernetes gRPC production work.
question.anchor: mitigated HTTP/2 TCP head-of-line blocking and L4 kube-proxy connection pinning on gRPC telemetry collectors via Envoy L7 ring-hash balancing

answers.label: excellent
answers.text: While HTTP/2 eliminates application-layer head-of-line (HOL) blocking by interleaving frames from multiple logical streams over one TCP connection, the underlying Linux kernel TCP stack remains strictly an ordered byte stream with no awareness of HTTP/2 stream boundaries. If a single TCP packet carrying a frame for Stream A is dropped on the network, the kernel cannot deliver subsequent already-arrived packets belonging to independent Streams B and C to userspace until Stream A's lost segment is retransmitted and acknowledged, stalling every multiplexed request on that socket and collapsing the TCP congestion window (`cwnd`). Furthermore, in Kubernetes, standard ClusterIP `kube-proxy` operates at L4 (TCP connection creation): because gRPC reuses a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection, all RPCs from a client pod get pinned to a single backend pod while newly scaled pods sit idle. On our gRPC telemetry ingestion tier handling 120k spans/sec, a 0.2% cross-AZ packet loss rate combined with L4 connection pinning caused periodic 400ms p99 latency spikes and uneven CPU saturation (85% on two pods vs 15% on six others). We solved both by deploying Envoy proxy sidecars configured for L7 gRPC request-level load balancing with a connection pool of 4 HTTP/2 connections per upstream endpoint, distributing both RPC load and packet-loss blast radius evenly and cutting p99 latency from 410ms to 19ms.

answers.text: HTTP/2 solves HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking by multiplexing multiple requests as streams over a single TCP connection, but it introduces TCP-level head-of-line blocking. Because TCP guarantees strict in-order byte delivery, if one TCP packet is lost, the operating system holds back all subsequent packets on that connection until the lost packet is retransmitted—blocking every HTTP/2 stream sharing that socket. Additionally, because gRPC keeps a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection open, Kubernetes' default L4 `kube-proxy` pins all traffic from a client to a single backend pod instead of balancing individual RPCs. On our gRPC telemetry collectors, we fixed this by introducing Envoy L7 load balancing with multiple connections per upstream pod.

cases.role_context: Senior LLM Inference Engineer — Model Serving & GPU Optimization

question.question: Explain how KV-cache memory fragmentation limits LLM serving batch sizes, how PagedAttention addresses it, and what trade-offs you encountered tuning vLLM prefix caching for your multi-turn coding assistant.
question.rationale: Tests deep understanding of autoregressive transformer inference mechanics, GPU HBM allocation, PagedAttention block tables, and real operational tuning.
question.anchor: tuned vLLM PagedAttention block sizes and APC (Automatic Prefix Caching) on H100 cluster doubling concurrent coding-agent throughput

answers.label: excellent
answers.text: During autoregressive LLM decoding, each generated token requires attending to the Key and Value tensors of all preceding tokens, which are cached in GPU HBM to avoid quadratic recomputation. Because output sequence lengths are unknown ahead of time, naive serving engines pre-allocate a contiguous HBM buffer sized to `max_seq_len` (e.g., 32k tokens) per request. This causes severe internal fragmentation (unused slots reserved for future tokens) and external fragmentation between variable-sized contiguous allocations, wasting 60–80% of KV-cache memory and starving the scheduler's continuous batching capacity. PagedAttention solves this by borrowing operating-system virtual memory paging: it partitions the KV cache into fixed-size non-contiguous physical KV blocks (e.g., 16 tokens per block) mapped via a per-sequence logical block table, allocating new physical blocks on-demand only as tokens are generated and reducing waste to under 4% (strictly bounded by the last partially filled block). When tuning vLLM on H100 GPUs for our multi-turn coding assistant—where turns shared a 12k-token repository context prefix—enabling Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) allowed requests with identical SHA-256 block hashes to share physical KV blocks zero-copy. The critical trade-off was block size selection: switching from 16-token to 64-token blocks sped up FlashAttention kernel throughput by 11% on prefill, but lowered cache hit rates at diverging user edits; 32-token blocks gave the optimal Pareto frontier, cutting Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) p95 by 58% and doubling concurrent request throughput.

answers.text: In LLM inference, the KV cache stores attention keys and values for previous tokens in GPU memory so they aren't recomputed at every decoding step. Traditional serving systems pre-allocated contiguous memory up to the maximum context length for each request, wasting most of GPU memory to internal and external fragmentation and limiting batch size. PagedAttention in vLLM fixes this by splitting the KV cache into small fixed-size blocks that can be stored non-contiguously in GPU memory and tracked with a block table, similar to OS virtual memory pages. On our H100 coding assistant cluster, we also enabled vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching so multi-turn prompts shared physical KV blocks for the static codebase prefix, doubling our serving throughput.

cases.role_context: Mid-Level Android / Mobile Engineer — Media & Feed Performance

question.question: Explain how Android's garbage collector handles generational heap memory and why allocating bitmap transformations inside `RecyclerView.onBindViewHolder` caused UI jank in your social media feed.
question.rationale: Checks fundamental understanding of ART generational GC, allocation rates during 120Hz scroll frames, bitmap memory footprint, and practical fix grounded in their resume.
question.anchor: eliminated scroll hitching in Kotlin feed RecyclerView by replacing onBindViewHolder bitmap allocations with Coil bitmap-pool pre-sizing

answers.label: excellent
answers.text: Android Runtime (ART) uses a concurrent copying generational garbage collector that divides the heap into a Young Generation (for newly allocated short-lived objects) and an Old/Large-Object Space. Most small objects die young and are reclaimed cheaply during minor GC sweeps, whereas large byte arrays and `Bitmap` pixel buffers exceeding the large-object threshold (typically 12KB) bypass the young nursery or trigger rapid heap footprint growth that forces frequent concurrent mark-compact cycles and short stop-the-world thread pauses. In our Kotlin social feed, `RecyclerView.onBindViewHolder` fires directly on the main UI thread every time a new card scrolls into the viewport—which on a 120Hz display leaves only 8.33ms per frame. The legacy code was instantiating a new `Canvas` and calling `Bitmap.createBitmap()` inside `onBindViewHolder` to apply rounded corners and aspect-ratio crops on each bound avatar and post image, allocating ~4MB of native/heap pixel buffers per fast fling. This spiked young/large-object GC throughput, stole CPU cores from the `RenderThread`, and caused 24ms frame hitches in Perfetto traces. I removed all allocation and transformation work from `onBindViewHolder` by configuring Coil with a shared `BitmapPool` (`inBitmap` reuse), downsampling images to exact view dimensions asynchronously on `Dispatchers.Default`, and delegating rounded corners to hardware-accelerated `ViewOutlineProvider` clipping on the GPU, dropping janky frames from 18% to 0.4%.

answers.text: Android's ART runtime uses a generational garbage collector where new objects are allocated in the young generation and large objects like bitmaps consume significant heap space. Because `RecyclerView.onBindViewHolder` runs on the main UI thread every time a row scrolls into view, creating new `Bitmap` objects for image cropping or rounded corners inside `onBindViewHolder` causes heavy memory churn during fast scrolling. This triggers frequent garbage collection pauses that block the main thread past the 16ms or 8ms frame deadline, resulting in visible scroll jank. In our Kotlin feed, I fixed this by offloading image decoding and sizing to background threads with Coil's bitmap pool reuse and using hardware view outlines for rounded corners.
